### StatLens Exercises {.unnumbered}

Let [StatLens]({{< var tool-url >}}){target="_blank"} do the arithmetic; spend your effort on the reasoning a calculator can't do.

1.  **The empirical rule, checked against the actual normal.** Open the [Normal tool]({{< var tool-url >}}/distribution/normal/?mu=0&sigma=1&tail=middle){target="_blank"} preset to $\mu = 0, \sigma = 1$.

    a.  Set the middle-region boundaries to $\pm 1$. What is the area? Is it 68%?
    b.  Now $\pm 2$. Is it 95%?
    c.  Now $\pm 3$. Is it 99.7%?
    d.  The empirical rule says "68--95--99.7." Where do the exact percentages come from --- the rule or the curve?


2.  **Standardizing across different normals.** Adult resting heart rates are approximately $N(\mu = 72, \sigma = 12)$ beats per minute. Adult body temperatures are approximately $N(\mu = 98.6, \sigma = 0.7)$ °F.

    a.  A patient has a heart rate of 90. What is her $z$-score?
    b.  A patient has a body temperature of 99.6 °F. What is his $z$-score?
    c.  Which patient is *more* unusual relative to their respective population? Why does the $z$-score answer this even though the two measurements are in different units?
    d.  Use the standard normal $z$ tool to find the percentile rank of each patient (the area to the left of their $z$-score). Are they in roughly the same percentile?


3.  **Inverse-normal (working backward).** A standardized test has scores $\sim N(500, 100)$.

    a.  What score corresponds to the **top 10%** of test-takers? Use the normal tool to set the right-tail area to 0.10 and read off the boundary.
    b.  What score is at the **25th percentile**? Use the left-tail area of 0.25.
    c.  What is the **interquartile range** of the score distribution?
    d.  A scholarship is offered to students scoring above the **90th percentile**. The college says: "Half of our applicants miss out by 50 points or fewer." Is this surprising, given the distribution?


4.  **Within vs. between normals --- a common confusion.** A factory measures the diameters of bolts. The population of individual diameters is $N(\mu = 10.0\text{ mm}, \sigma = 0.05\text{ mm})$. The quality team measures samples of $n = 25$ bolts at a time and computes the sample mean diameter $\bar{x}$.

    a.  Find $P(\text{individual bolt} > 10.10\text{ mm})$ using the [normal tool at $\mu = 10, \sigma = 0.05$]({{< var tool-url >}}/distribution/normal/?mu=10&sigma=0.05&tail=right){target="_blank"}.
    b.  Find $P(\bar{x} > 10.10\text{ mm})$ using the [normal tool at the *sampling-distribution* parameters]({{< var tool-url >}}/distribution/normal/?mu=10&sigma=0.01&tail=right){target="_blank"} ($\mu = 10$, $\sigma_{\bar{x}} = 0.05/\sqrt{25} = 0.01$).
    c.  Which is smaller, and by how much? Why does the same threshold (10.10 mm) become much more "extreme" for $\bar{x}$ than for an individual bolt?
    d.  A quality engineer says: "We never see sample means above 10.10 mm --- the process is in control." How would you push back if the **individual-bolt** rate of "above 10.10" is 2%?


5.  **The normal distribution as a model --- not reality.** Heights of adult males are *approximately* normal. Hourly wages in a population are *not*.

    a.  Why is **height** well-modeled by a normal --- and what feature of the data-generating process makes it so?
    b.  Why are **hourly wages** typically *not* well-modeled by a normal? Sketch the shape you'd expect.
    c.  Suppose you use a normal model anyway to predict wage percentiles. What kind of errors are you likely to make?
    d.  When does the normal still help, even when the underlying variable isn't normal? (Hint: think back to the sampling distributions chapter.)
